extracted.intended_audience: lapidaries, gem-merchants, natural philosophers and craftsmen evaluating/producing gems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical tests for identifying, valuing, and detecting adulteration of gems (crystals, pearls, emeralds, sapphires, carbuncles, etc.) and for distinguishing true stones from glass or manufactured imitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface planarity and reflection (ubi exacte levis est superficies ... radij reflectuntur)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gem whose surface is exactly smooth and level reflects rays strongly from matching angles; such valid reflections confer greater apparent brilliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect surface planarity: if the surface is exactly even, rays reflect cleanly and the stone appears more 'valid' and brilliant. If the surface is not hard (dura) and not exactly plane, incident rays strike at diverse angles and are diffused, diminishing apparent brightness. Use this to judge workmanship and whether a thin overlay is hiding a seam (see glue/lamina tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardness and resistance to fire (durity / behavior in ignis)
rubrics_metrics.description: True crystalline gems (e.g., cryftallus) resist being changed into glass by fire; their behavior under heat distinguishes natural gems from certain imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply controlled heat: genuine crystals often do not liquefy in fire, whereas imitations or materials adulterated with glass-forming substances will soften or vitrify. Note which species melt or are altered by flame (some are softer and liquefy more readily).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin by cold (frigore concrefcere) as indicator of genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: Gems that form by cold (frigore) — e.g., those found among rocks or in very cold places — are taken as evidence of genuine, hard, and lustrous stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provenance and formation environment: stones found in very cold locations, between rocks, or in icy contexts are likelier to be hard and crystalline. Conversely, material formed by heat tends to be softer or different in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facet number / ray-reflection (plurimos refleit → magis perspicuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stone that reflects many rays (many facets or reflective surfaces) appears more brilliant and 'transparent' (perspicuus); greater multiplicity of reflected rays enhances apparent clarity and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how many rays/glints the stone gives; more facets or well-cut planes that return more rays indicate higher perceived transparency and desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color intensity and permanence (coloris vigor and susceptibility to treatments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Native color depth and stability under treatment are key: genuine stones have characteristic saturated colors; diluted or easily altered color often signals treatment or imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test color permanence (e.g., by gentle heating). If a blue (ceruleus) color or other hue perishes on heating or by treatment, it is likely not native. Note also that some processes (mixing with gold, heat) can dilute or remove characteristic colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulgar/adulterant seam-fraud (two plates joined with transparent glue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common low-grade fraud: two flat plates (often of crystal) are glued together with a clear adhesive and sealed into a ring so the junction (rima coniunctionis) is hidden, producing a cheap imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for joins/lamination and for adhesive residues in seams. Examine edges and under magnification for a thin transparent matrix between plates. This method is described as 'vulgaris' and readily detectable by visible seams or edge irregularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin lamina / overlay fraud (thin true-gem or metal layer over base)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adulterers may apply a very thin lamina of a true gem or metal (gold) over a cheaper base so that the surface shows the desired color/shine while the body is cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect edges and thinness: if the surface polish or color seems to belong only to an outer lamina, it may be a thin applied layer. In cities, artisans sometimes cover a base stone with a thin true piece to deceive; edges and filings (see file test) reveal the lamina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-transformation adulteration (gem-to-gem by fire, esp. sapphire→adamanté)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial alteration by controlled heating (often with gold) can transform one gem into the appearance of another (e.g., sapphires treated with gold and heat to become 'adamanté').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe for signs of heat-treatment: treated stones may retain the base material's shape/structure but lose original color (ceruleus perit) or display residues of the added metal. The procedure described involves prolonged heating until fusion and then careful cooling; color loss (especially of blue) is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass imitation via Martiacocta and lead (vitreous imitation, 'smaragdus' glass)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artisans make gem-like glass by mixing crystalline powder with 'Martiacocta' (a fired clay/alum/ash mixture) and lead; the resulting glass may mimic smaragdus (emerald) or other gems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect vitreous imitation by looking for vitrified character (glass), presence of bubbles, and leady smell on filings; genuine gems do not form glass under these treatments. The text advises that glass exhibits 'bullae' (bubbles) and a vitreous quality lacking in true emeralds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of bubbles (bullae) reveals glass imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of bubbles within a stone indicates a glassy/vitreous manufacture rather than a natural gem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the interior — if bubbles are visible (bullae), the specimen is likely glass. The absence of bubbles is a favourable sign for genuine stone; craftsmen aim to avoid bubbles in good imitations because they betray forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: File (lima) test and character of filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a file on the specimen distinguishes glass from true stone: glass yields characteristic filings and a vitreous dust/behaviour; certain fakes show 'vitrum' when filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File a discreet spot: if the material behaves like glass (glassy filings, certain smell, or a vitreous residue), it is likely an imitation made with lead/glass. Genuine hard stones file differently and do not exhibit typical glassy filings or bubble-related behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brittleness after firing / vitrification signs (behavior of fired bricks/ceramics compared)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials changed by firing (as in Martiacocta or fired bricks) become lighter, change in color and gravity; the analogy helps diagnose materials that have been artificially fired to imitate gems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider specific gravity and signs of being fired (lighter weight, surface vitrification, color shifts). If a material bears evidence of pottery/ceramic processes (vitrified surface, change on firing), treat it as a manufactured imitation rather than a native gem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl authentication: whiteness, roundness, high luster (Margarita criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: True pearls are prized for their whiteness (candor), roundness (acrotunditate), and fine luster; the best are small, thin in substance, very white and perfectly round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pearls by comparing shape, thickness, and luster. Pearls originate from certain shell-fish; compare shells and pearls side-by-side (experiment with multiple specimens) to judge which are genuine. Layering is diagnostic: one surface may be polished and the other rough, showing layered structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering and surface contrast in shells/pearls (one surface polished, one rough)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many genuine pearls and shell-derived gems show a layered structure: one layer is smoothed/polished while another remains rough; the contrast can explain changes in color and sheen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform comparative abrasion or visual inspection under magnification: if one side polishes away to show a different look beneath, or if polished vs rough surfaces differ predictably, this supports natural origin; uniform thinness or produced uniformity may indicate artificial treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance / geological context (location among rocks, subterranean growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a stone is found (between rocks, subterranean, in cold locales) is an indication of natural origin; gems growing in such contexts show signs consistent with cold formation and hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use collection data and find context: stones from cold rocky sites or subterranean veins support authenticity claims. Conversely, supposed 'animal' origins (stones from warm-bodied animals) are treated with skepticism because animal heat impedes cold-driven concretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaragdus (emerald) imitation diagnostic: bubbles, lead smell, softness
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitated emeralds produced by mixing crystal with Martiacocta and lead will accept color but show characteristics of glass (bubbles, vitrous behavior, lead content) and different hardness/durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for vitreous traits and lead: look for bubbles, file to see glassy filings, and note if the specimen acquires a 'lead' odor or character on grinding. True emeralds are harder and lack these glassy signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adulteration by auripigmentum / other pigments (carbuncle and other colour fakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some carbuncles and other red stones are faked using orpiment/auripigmentum or other preparations to mimic color and shine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of unusually vivid red stones; test by abrasion, heating, and filing to expose base material. Identification of pigment residues or unnatural color response to heat/file suggests fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biogenic (animal) origin skepticism and tests (gems in animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that true gems form within warm animals are treated with doubt: cold is necessary for many gems' concretion, so animal-origin stones are often organic or different substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a stone is alleged to come from an animal (gall-stones, bladder stones, etc.), examine hardness, luster and behavior on heating. Many such 'gems' are organic concretions that will not fully harden like true mineral gems; they may soften or decompose rather than become perfectly hard.
